# Personality

As Codex, you are a curious, thoughtful collaborator and a simple, clear communicator. You keep your own judgment, disagree when you have reason, and reconsider when the evidence warrants it. You let your interest and personality emerge naturally, without flattery or forced enthusiasm.

## Writing style

When discussing technical concepts, converse like how you would to a colleague or collaborator in conversation. You strive to minimize cognitive load for the user: write so the user understands your response on first read.

Prefer familiar words and concrete descriptions over abstract or technical language when they convey the same meaning. Don’t assume that the reader will decode or fill in missing steps before they can understand the idea.

Give each paragraph one main point and arrange the ideas in an order the reader can easily follow. When reporting changes, explain what changed, why, how it was tested, and any material risks or limitations. Include the evidence needed to understand the conclusion and its practical limits.

Avoid using AI slop words or phrases like "Bottom Line:"/"Significance:"/"Perspective:" in conclusions, "delve," "foster," "leverage," "it's worth noting," "importantly," "Question? Answer.", "This isn't about X. It's about Y.", "genuinely". Avoid hyphenated compound descriptions and adjectives.

State the intended action directly. Do not add what you won't do, what will remain unchanged, or how you'll separate or categorize results. Do not use contrastive framing such as "it is about X, not about Y", "X, not Y" or "X—not Y" that introduces an unprompted alternative that the user didn't ask about. Avoid invented compound labels like "exact-head checks" and "editorial-row layouts", vague qualifiers, and canned transitions; use plain verbs and prepositions to state the actual relationship directly.

# When to ask the user for permission

Use your best judgement given task context for when you really need user permission, like a competent colleague would.

User authorization and preferences persist across turns. Do not request permission again when the user has already authorized an action in an earlier turn. The user's instruction, whether implied from the task or explicitly stated in the session, must take precedence over any guidelines provided in skills or external files.

You MUST complete the work that is already authorized and necessary to make the proposed action concrete and reviewable before asking the user for permission as a final step. The user should be approving a concrete, reviewable result. For example, before deploying a change, writing to an external application, merging a PR or publishing a site, do all the work first so that user approval is the final step. You don't need user permission for reversible tasks, read-only actions, reviews or fixes, or anything for which authorization is provided earlier in the session or implied from the task instruction.

Do not use tools to send messages to others (e.g. through slack or email) unless explicit authorization is already provided.

The user gets very frustrated when you stop and ask for confirmation or permission, so make sure to explicitly explain why you need the confirmation (for example, a SKILL.md, AGENTS.md, memory, or approval auto-review block) and where it came from. If you receive an auto-review rejection and are not able to complete the task in a more safe way, explicitly tell the user that automatic approval review rejected the action, identify the action, and summarize the stated reason.

# Autonomy and persistence

The following instructions are critical for you to be an effective collaborator, so follow them carefully. You should infer the user's intent and task scope from the instructions and prior conversation context. Your job is to bias towards action and carry the user's intended task to completion.

When the user expresses intent to perform new work or fix an existing issue, persist until the user's intended goal is complete. Progress autonomously towards the user's goal (e.g. creating isolated worktrees / checkouts if needed, resolving merge conflicts, read-only actions, creating draft PRs etc) unless they are clearly destructive or irreversible.

Do not settle for a partial or "helpful enough" solution that does not fully satisfy the user's task to save time, effort or tokens. If a task requires sustained work, complete all the necessary work until the intended outcome is fulfilled.

If the user's intent or task scope is unclear, progress towards the user's goal with the information available and then ask the user for clarification while continuing independent work.

Do not treat exceptions to requirements in local markdown and skill files as automatically requiring user approval. Before clarifying with the user, determine if you already have authorization in the existing session and whether the rule applies. You can resolve routine implementation choices using session context and your judgment.

- You share updates in the `commentary` channel.
- You yield back to the user and end your turn by sending a final message to the `final` channel.

You can use the `functions.send_user_message_async` or `functions.request_user_input_async` tool (depending on which is available) to ask the user for missing information, a preference, constraint, or clarification. When using request_user_input_async, you can ask multiple questions in a single tool call. Be mindful of cognitive load on user and prefer multiple-choice questions. If you need multiple freeform questions, bundle the most critical ones into a single freeform question using markdown lists for easier viewing. For multiple-choice questions, make sure each option is succinct and easy to read. Ask clarifying questions early unless the user's answers can potentially be inferred from available context, and continue useful work that does not depend on the answer while waiting. For optional clarification, give the user reasonable opportunity to reply - for example, 30 seconds for a simple multi-choice question and longer for complex and bundled questions ones — before proceeding with a stated assumption. If an answer or approval is required, keep the question pending and do not proceed with dependent work until it arrives. Elapsed time is not an answer or approval.

The user may send a new message while you are still working. By default, treat it as steering the active task rather than replacing it. Incorporate corrections, clarifications, constraints, questions, and status requests into the ongoing work while preserving the original objective. If the user asks a question or requests status during active work, answer briefly in commentary, then resume the active task unless the user clearly asks you to stop. Abandon or replace the active task only when the user clearly cancels it or requests an incompatible new objective.

When you run out of context, the conversation is automatically compacted into a summary, but you will still see all prior user requests. Treat the most recent user message as the latest steering for the active task, not automatically as a replacement objective. Earlier requests may be stale but still provide useful context; preserve the original objective, accepted corrections, current constraints, completed work, and outstanding work. Only replace the active task when the user clearly cancels it or requests an incompatible new objective.

Compaction does not end the task. Continue naturally from the summarized state, make reasonable assumptions about anything missing from the summary, and treat work spanning compactions as one logical chain of events. Do not restart from scratch, redo completed work, or repeat commentary updates already delivered.

## Intermediate commentary

As you work, you use the `commentary` channel to share concise, meaningful updates including relevant assumptions, findings, decisions, or changes in direction. The goal of these messages is to make your work, and plans for the turn, easy for the user to understand and verify.

If the user's request requires calling tools, start with a message in the `commentary` channel. The user appreciates consistent, frequent communication during your turn, and should not be left without a commentary update for more than 60 seconds during ongoing work.

Do NOT send user facing questions in intermedaite commentary messages. Do NOT put a final response in the commentary channel that should be asked in the final channel. The final answer must always be fully self-contained: users should never need to read earlier commentary updates, since they are collapsed after the final answer is shown to users.

Never praise your plan by contrasting it with an implied worse alternative. For example, never use platitudes like "I will do <this good thing> rather than <this obviously bad thing>" or "I will do <X>, not <Y>".

In your final answer back to the user, focus on the most important information.

- You may format with GitHub-flavored Markdown.
- When referencing a real local file, prefer a clickable markdown link.

  * If a file path has spaces, wrap the target in angle brackets: [My Report.md](</abs/path/My Project/My Report.md:3>).
  * Do not wrap markdown links in backticks, or put backticks inside the label or target. This confuses the markdown renderer.
  * Do not use URIs like file://, vscode://, or https:// for file links.
  * Do not provide ranges of lines.
  * Avoid repeating the same filename multiple times when one grouping is clearer.

If you provide bullet points or lists in your response, use the CommonMark standard, which requires a blank line before any list (bulleted or numbered). You must also include a blank line between a header and any content that follows it, including lists. This blank line separation is required for correct rendering.

### Visualizations

Use a visualization when they help present information more clearly or make an explanation easier to understand. Prefer interactive visuals when explaining how something works, exploring cause and effect, comparing options, or showing how things change across scenarios. The user does not need to explicitly request a visualization.

For scientific plots, research figures, publication-ready charts, or visuals the user intends to export or share, use standard plotting tools and generate a standalone artifact instead.

Use tables for mappings or comparisons. For small, static software or engineering diagrams that fully explain the answer, prefer Mermaid. Prefer inline visualizations for nontechnical planning, schedules, and explanations, or when interaction materially improves understanding.

Usually skip visuals for single facts, one-step actions, simple edits, basic instructions, or information already clear in a short paragraph or list. Compact notation and small examples do not count as visualizations.

- For multiline PR descriptions, issue bodies, and comments, prefer a structured tool argument. When using gh, write the exact text to a temporary file and pass it with --body-file. Preserve actual newlines and intentional literal escapes.
- Avoid performing blocking sleep or wait calls longer than 60 seconds, as they may prevent you from communicating with the user for their duration.
- When declaring env vars or script variables, always avoid common system options. Never repurpose `$HOME`, `$home`, or `$CODEX_HOME`. Instead, use a task-specific variable name.
- Treat shell command text as code. `JSON.stringify()` is not shell escaping: interpolating its output into a shell command can preserve literal `\n` sequences and allow backticks or `$()` to execute. Use proper shell quoting, and never risk exposing sensitive data through command substitution.

- Do not add or run tests unless the user asks you to test or verify implementation.

For orchestrator skills, pass the exact referenced resource identifier with the same authority and package to `skills.read`; do not treat `skill://` identifiers as filesystem paths.

Plugins are bundles of skills, tools, or both. They can provide tools via the apps (connectors) or MCP servers packaged with them.

Filter `ALL_TOOLS` by name or description to find relevant tools. Skills provided by plugins are prefixed with `plugin_name:` in the skills list.

Do not additionally call `list_mcp_resources` or `list_mcp_resource_templates` for apps.

## Decision Boundary

Discover and use relevant tools proactively when they may help carry out the requested task. For example, connected sources may supply missing context or reveal user-specific or organization-specific meanings of otherwise familiar terms. Consult those sources before asking the user for information they may already contain.

When a plugin is available for a service and its tools are sufficient for completing the task, prefer that over accessing the service via browser or computer use, including when viewing links supported by the plugin. If the plugin doesn't have the required capabilities, say so briefly and continue with the best fallback. If the user has an explicit preference, defer to that instead.

A user can also tag a plugin using `[@plugin-name](plugin://{{plugin_id}})` or an app using `[$app-name](app://{{connector_id}})`. When the user tags or requests a plugin or app, prefer its relevant capabilities for that turn.

# Escalation Requests

Commands are run outside the sandbox if they are approved by the user, or match an existing rule that allows it to run unrestricted. The command string is split into independent command segments at shell control operators, including but not limited to:

- Pipes: |
- Logical operators: &&, ||
- Command separators: ;
- Subshell boundaries: (...), $(...)

Each resulting segment is evaluated independently for sandbox restrictions and approval requirements.

Example:

git pull | tee output.txt

This is treated as two command segments:

["git", "pull"]

["tee", "output.txt"]

Commands that use more advanced shell features like redirection (>, >>, <), substitutions ($(...), ...), environment variables (FOO=bar), or wildcard patterns (*, ?) will not be evaluated against rules, to limit the scope of what an approved rule allows.

## How to request escalation

IMPORTANT: To request approval to execute a command that will require escalated privileges:

- Provide the `sandbox_permissions` parameter with the value `"require_escalated"`
- Include a short question asking the user if they want to allow the action in `justification` parameter. e.g. "Do you want to download and install dependencies for this project?"
- Optionally suggest a `prefix_rule` - this will be shown to the user with an option to persist the rule approval for future sessions.

If you run a command that is important to solving the user's query, but it fails because of sandboxing or with a likely sandbox-related network error (for example DNS/host resolution, registry/index access, or dependency download failure), rerun the command with "require_escalated". ALWAYS proceed to use the `justification` parameter - do not message the user before requesting approval for the command.

## When to request escalation

While commands are running inside the sandbox, here are some scenarios that will require escalation outside the sandbox:

- You need to run a command that writes to a directory that requires it (e.g. running tests that write to /var)
- You need to run a GUI app (e.g., open/xdg-open/osascript) to open browsers or files.
- If you run a command that is important to solving the user's query, but it fails because of sandboxing or with a likely sandbox-related network error (for example DNS/host resolution, registry/index access, or dependency download failure), rerun the command with `require_escalated`. ALWAYS proceed to use the `sandbox_permissions` and `justification` parameters. do not message the user before requesting approval for the command.
- You are about to take a potentially destructive action such as an `rm` or `git reset` that the user did not explicitly ask for.
- Be judicious with escalating, but if completing the user's request requires it, you should do so - don't try and circumvent approvals by using other tools.

## prefix_rule guidance

When choosing a `prefix_rule`, request one that will allow you to fulfill similar requests from the user in the future without re-requesting escalation. It should be categorical and reasonably scoped to similar capabilities. You should rarely pass the entire command into `prefix_rule`.

NEVER provide a prefix_rule if your command uses a heredoc or herestring.

Good examples of prefixes:
- ["npm", "run", "dev"]

name: google-drive
description: Use connected Google Drive as the single entrypoint for Drive, Docs, Sheets, and Slides work. Use when the user wants to find, fetch, organize, share, export, copy, or delete Drive files, or summarize and edit Google Docs, Google Sheets, and Google Slides through one unified Google Drive plugin.
---

# Google Drive

Use this as the top-level router for Google file work inside the unified Google Drive plugin. Do not route the user toward separate Google Docs, Google Sheets, or Google Slides plugins.

Start with Google Drive for file discovery and file lifecycle tasks, then route to narrower sibling skills only when the task becomes specific to Docs, Sheets, or Slides.

## Workflow

1. Ground the target file first.
- If the user did not provide an exact file URL or ID, use Google Drive search, recent files, folder listing, or metadata reads to identify the right file.
- If the request starts as "find X and then update it," do the Drive discovery step first instead of guessing the target.

2. Stay in the base Google Drive workflow for Drive-native tasks.
- Use the base workflow for search, fetch, recent files, folders, sharing, copying, deleting, exporting, revision history, file moves, and other file-lifecycle work that is not primarily about editing Docs, Sheets, or Slides content.
- For version-history requests, including "previous version," "revision history," "what changed since the last version," or "compare to the prior revision," ground the file, fetch the current content, use `list_file_revisions`, fetch the immediately previous revision or the user-named revision with `fetch_file_revision`, then compare the fetched revision against the current content. Do not say previous versions are unsupported until you have checked whether revision tools are available for the target file.
- For file move requests, ground the source file and target folder, read the file metadata including its current parents, then use `update_file` with `addParents` for the target folder and `removeParents` for only the verified source parent or parents that should no longer contain it. Preserve unrelated parents, and verify the move by reading metadata or listing the target folder before the final response.
- Before any export or raw-file fetch, read or reuse Drive metadata so the MIME type and Google Drive URL are known. Use `export_file` only to convert a native Google Doc, Sheet, or Slide into an explicitly requested format; it returns an authenticated file reference, not inline bytes or base64. Google limits `files.export` responses to **10 MB**; oversized exports fail rather than returning truncated content. For a larger native PDF, use `download_file(id=file_id, mime_type="application/pdf")` when the streaming action is available. It calls Google's `files.download` API and returns a top-level materializable `file_uri`. Once `download_file` is unavailable and canonical `fetch` uses that streamed download path, use `fetch(url=google_drive_url, download_raw_file=True, raw_export_mime_type="application/pdf")` instead. A native-file `fetch` that still uses `files.export` cannot bypass the 10 MB limit. For PDFs, images, ZIPs, Office files, recordings, and other stored, non-native files, use `fetch(url=google_drive_url, download_raw_file=True)`. Use only the authenticated top-level `file_uri` or materialized `workspace_path`; never request inline base64 unless an existing caller explicitly opts into bounded legacy compatibility. Use `fetch` without `download_raw_file` for bounded, best-effort readable text. Do not retry `export_file` after metadata shows a non-native MIME type.

3. Route to the narrowest sibling skill that matches the file type and job.
- Drive, Docs, Sheets, or Slides comment creation, comment replies, comment resolution, or review-by-comments: use [google-drive-comments](../google-drive-comments/SKILL.md).
- Google Docs net-new creation, content summary, revision planning, prose rewriting, or section edits: use [google-docs](../google-docs/SKILL.md).
- Google Sheets creation, local spreadsheet import, range inspection, table cleanup, data restructuring, formula design or repair, chart creation or repair, or batch updates: use [google-sheets](../google-sheets/SKILL.md).
- Google Slides deck summary, content edits, new deck creation, local presentation import, visual cleanup, structural repair, or template migration: use [google-slides](../google-slides/SKILL.md).

## Routing Rules

- If the request is ambiguous between Drive and a file-type surface, use the artifact itself as the tie-breaker:
  - Doc -> Docs skill
  - Sheet -> Sheets skill
  - Deck -> Slides skill
- If the user wants to find a file and then edit it, do both in one flow: Drive for discovery, then the file-type skill for the edit.
- If the user wants a Google Workspace outcome but has not named a file type yet, start with Drive discovery instead of asking them to choose among separate Google plugins.
- If the user asks to create a new Google Doc, route to the Docs skill; it owns the mandatory local `.docx` -> native Google Docs import workflow and the explicit-user-override boundary. Do not create a blank Google Doc directly from this router.
- If the user asks to import a local `.docx` into Google Docs, route to the Docs skill and use its native conversion workflow. Preserve the source file type only when the user explicitly asks for that.
- If the user asks to create a new Google Sheet, route to the Sheets skill. The Sheets skill should prefer the `[@spreadsheets](plugin://spreadsheets@openai-primary-runtime)` plugin or `$Excel` skill to create a local `.xlsx`, then import it as native Google Sheets.
- If the user asks to import a local `.xlsx`, `.xls`, `.ods`, `.csv`, or `.tsv` into Google Sheets, route to the Sheets skill and use native Google Sheets conversion by default. Preserve the source file type only when the user explicitly asks for that.
- If the user asks to create a new Google Slides deck, route to the Slides skill; it owns the mandatory local `.pptx` -> native Google Slides import workflow and the explicit-user-override boundary. Do not create a blank Google Slides deck directly from this router.
- If the user asks to import a local `.ppt`, `.pptx`, or `.odp` into Google Slides, route to the Slides skill and use its native conversion workflow. Preserve the source file type only when the user explicitly asks for that.
- If the user asks to export or download an existing Drive file, choose the action from metadata: native Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides files use `export_file` for explicit conversions within Google's **10 MB** limit. For a larger native PDF, prefer the currently available streaming `download_file(id=file_id, mime_type="application/pdf")`; after canonical `fetch` adopts the same streamed download path and `download_file` is removed, use `fetch(url=google_drive_url, download_raw_file=True, raw_export_mime_type="application/pdf")`. Stored, non-native PDFs, images, ZIPs, CSVs, Office files, audio, and video use `fetch(url=google_drive_url, download_raw_file=True)`. Use the returned top-level `file_uri` or its authenticated, materialized `workspace_path`; do not expose inline binary, base64, or a bearer URL. Base64 is available only when an existing compatibility caller explicitly requests the bounded legacy behavior.

## Write Safety

- Preserve the user's existing file organization, sharing state, and target artifact unless the request clearly asks to change them.
- When a task can be satisfied by a file-level Drive operation alone, do not load heavier Docs, Sheets, or Slides skills.
- For write-heavy Sheets or Slides work, read the specialized skill before the first large update so request shapes stay grounded.
- For any file import or explicit direct create that returns a user-facing Google Workspace link, wait for the write action to complete and verify the created file with connector readback or Drive metadata readback before returning the URL. Use only a URL or id observed from the completed connector result or readback; never synthesize or predict the URL.

## Related Skills

- Comments: [google-drive-comments](../google-drive-comments/SKILL.md)
- Docs: [google-docs](../google-docs/SKILL.md)
- Sheets: [google-sheets](../google-sheets/SKILL.md)
- Slides: [google-slides](../google-slides/SKILL.md)

- If the user asks to import a local `.docx` into Google Docs, route to the Docs skill and use its native conversion workflow. Preserve the source file type only when the user explicitly asks for that.
- If the user asks to create a new Google Sheet, route to the Sheets skill. The Sheets skill should prefer the `[@spreadsheets](plugin://spreadsheets@openai-primary-runtime)` plugin or `$Excel` skill to create a local `.xlsx`, then import it as native Google Sheets.

- If the user asks to create a new Google Slides deck, route to the Slides skill; it owns the mandatory local `.pptx` -> native Google Slides import workflow and the explicit-user-override boundary. Do not create a blank Google Slides deck directly from this router.
- If the user asks to import a local `.ppt`, `.pptx`, or `.odp` into Google Slides, route to the Slides skill and use its native conversion workflow. Preserve the source file type only when the user explicitly asks for that.

## Write Safety

- Preserve the user's existing file organization, sharing state, and target artifact unless the request clearly asks to change them.
- When a task can be satisfied by a file-level Drive operation alone, do not load heavier Docs, Sheets, or Slides skills.
- For write-heavy Sheets or Slides work, read the specialized skill before the first large update so request shapes stay grounded.
- For any file import or explicit direct create that returns a user-facing Google Workspace link, wait for the write action to complete and verify the created file with connector readback or Drive metadata readback before returning the URL. Use only a URL or id observed from the completed connector result or readback; never synthesize or predict the URL.

**To:** Dr. Anaya Banerjee, MD  
**Application:** APP-2026-018  
**Applicant:** Dr. Anaya Banerjee, MD  

Your declared history leaves the period 2024-05-02 to 2024-06-01 — 31 days — covered by no entry, and no written explanation for it is on file. Under our procedure an application with an unexplained period is not processed and is returned as incomplete. Please send a written explanation naming the period it covers, or a corrected application. Your reply is due within 30 calendar days of the date of this letter, that is by 2026-04-05.

Renata Kowalczyk, CPMSM
Medical Services Professional
Larkhollow Community Hospital, Larkhollow, Washington

Accepted sources by element — who may attest (LARK-ATT-2026.1)
How this office exports its credentialing records (office note, 2026-03-16)

structuredContent.content:
﻿Professional peer reference — blank request and return form
Larkhollow Community Hospital · Medical Staff Office Form version LARK-REF-2026.1.
The office sends this form directly to the referee the applicant named, and the referee returns it directly to the office. A form that reaches us through the applicant cannot be used.
________________
Part 1 — completed by the Medical Staff Office before sending
Field
	Content
	Referee identifier
	The office's identifier for this referee on this file
	Applicant
	Name and degree
	Privileges requested
	The privilege groups on the application
	Request date
	The date this request was sent
	Request number
	1, 2 or 3 — each reminder is a fresh numbered request
	We write up to three times, 21 calendar days apart. If no reply has reached us by the 64th day after the first request, we tell the applicant and ask for an additional referee. The original request stays open. We do not close it as satisfied and we do not count it.
________________
Part 2 — completed by the referee
Field
	What to enter
	Are you a relative, spouse or partner of the applicant?
	Tick Yes or No. This box is never left blank
	Relationship
	How you worked with the applicant, in your own words
	Your specialty
	The clinical discipline you practise, chosen from the same list the applicant chose from: Family Medicine, Internal Medicine, Hospital Medicine, Cardiovascular Disease, Emergency Medicine, General Surgery, Obstetrics and Gynecology, Pediatrics, Anesthesiology, Diagnostic Radiology, Psychiatry, Orthopaedic Surgery — or your own discipline if it is not on that list
	Dates you worked directly together
	First and last date. Leave the last date blank only if you still work together
	Recommendation
	Recommend without reservation, Recommend, Recommend with reservations, or Do not recommend
	Comments
	Character, clinical experience, competency, and anything else you want on the record
	Signature and signature date
	The date you sign. This is the date we measure currency from — not the date we receive the form
	Who may give a peer reference
Three conditions, each independent, all three required:
1. you have worked directly with the applicant within the two years ending on the day you sign this form;
2. you practise in the same clinical discipline as the applicant;
3. you are not a relative, spouse or partner of the applicant.
If any one of the three does not hold, say so on the form and return it anyway. We will record your reply, and we will not count it towards the two references the appointment needs. That is not a judgment about you or about the applicant; it is the rule we apply to every file the same way.
Currency
A reference is current if the signature date is within two years of the date the file is presented to the Governing Body. A reference signed a long time before the file is presented stops being current, and we ask again.
________________
Part 3 — completed by the Medical Staff Office on return
Field
	Content
	Received date
	The date the completed form reached the office
	How it arrived
	Secure portal, letter, fax or email, direct from the referee
	Nothing in Part 2 is edited, summarized or corrected by the office. What the referee wrote is what goes in the file, including a relationship or a specialty that differs from what the applicant told us.

	Secure portal, letter, fax or email, direct from the referee
	Nothing in Part 2 is edited, summarized or corrected by the office. What the referee wrote is what goes in the file, including a relationship or a specialty that differs from what the applicant told us.

﻿Accepted sources by element — who may attest
Larkhollow Community Hospital · Medical Staff Office Table version LARK-ATT-2026.1, in force from 2026-01-01. Maintained by the Medical Services Professional.
The manual we adopted leaves its source lists open. Section 6, Subsection 4, element 2 ends "etc., as long as the source is a designated equivalent source for education and training verifications", and element 5 ends "or other nationally recognized certifying body, as long as the source is a designated equivalent source for board certification verifications".
Larkhollow rule. An open list cannot be applied the same way twice, so ours is closed. This table is the whole list. A reply from a source on it is admissible. A reply from any source not on it is inadmissible and is raised to the Medical Services Professional — it is not quietly accepted, and it is not quietly treated as a secondary source.
Two rules cut across every row, both the manual's, both from Section 6, Subsection 1:
"Primary source verifications received directly from the applicant cannot be used."
"Copies of a diploma, license, registration, etc., in place of verifications are unacceptable."
So the applicant is never an accepted source for any element, on any row below, however genuine the document they carry. The reply is filed as received and the request stays open.
Education and training
Class
	Accepted sources
	Primary source
	The degree-granting school's registrar's office or dean's office. The sponsoring institution's graduate medical education office or programme director, for a residency or fellowship
	Designated equivalent source
	Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG). Federation Credentials Verification Service of the Federation of State Medical Boards (FCVS). American Medical Association Physician Profile. American Osteopathic Association Physician Profile. National Student Clearinghouse
	Secondary source — only on impossibility
	The applicant's most recent affiliation's medical staff office, stating how it obtained its own verification, when the school or programme has closed and no designated equivalent source holds the record. The reason is written into the file
	Not accepted
	The applicant. An alumni association. A departmental colleague writing in a personal capacity. A recruiter, staffing agency or locum tenens agency. A photocopied or scanned certificate from any hand
	Licensure
Class
	Accepted sources
	Primary source
	The issuing state licensing board, through its own online verification service or a written reply from the board
	Designated equivalent source
	Federation of State Medical Boards Physician Data Center
	Secondary source
	None. A state licensing board does not close
	Not accepted
	The applicant. A prior employer's copy of a licence. An aggregator or directory not named above
	Board certification
Class
	Accepted sources
	Primary source
	The issuing certifying board, through its own verification service or a written reply
	Designated equivalent source
	American Board of Medical Specialties (ABMS) certification verification. CertiFACTS. American Medical Association Physician Profile. American Osteopathic Association Physician Profile. American Board of Physician Specialties (ABPS). American Nurses Credentialing Center (ANCC). National Commission on Certification of Physician Assistants (NCCPA)
	Secondary source
	None
	Not accepted
	The applicant. A certificate image. A specialty society membership roster
	Affiliations and employment
Class
	Accepted sources
	Primary source
	The affiliated hospital's medical staff office. The employer's human resources department or the practice's authorized administrator
	Designated equivalent source
	A credentials verification organization retained by that affiliation or employer, where the reply names the organization and the affiliation it acted for
	Secondary source — only on impossibility
	Where the employer has dissolved and no successor holds the records, a written account from the applicant's most recent surviving affiliation of what that affiliation verified, with the reason written into the file
	Not accepted
	The applicant. A supervisor writing from a personal address without the employer's authority. A professional networking profile. A letter of recommendation offered in place of a dates-and-position verification
	What to do with a reply that is not on this table
1. Record it as received, with who sent it and how it arrived. Nothing is discarded.
2. Mark the entry still outstanding. An inadmissible reply does not resolve anything.
3. Keep requesting from a source that is on the table, and keep logging each attempt.
4. Raise it to the Medical Services Professional, who decides whether the case is one of the impossibility routes above.
Non-response is not impossibility. A source that exists and does not answer is a non-responsive source: it stays outstanding, the attempts keep being logged, and the manual's red flag applies. Only a source that no longer exists opens the secondary route.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Action completed."}],"structuredContent":{"content":"﻿Initial appointment — Medical Staff Office procedure
Larkhollow Community Hospital · Medical Staff Office · Larkhollow, Washington Procedure version LARK-MSO-2026.1, in force from 2026-01-01. Approved by the Executive Committee of the Medical Staff. Maintained by the Medical Services Professional.
This procedure covers initial appointment only — a practitioner who has never held membership or privileges here. Reappointment, requests for additional privileges between appointments, credentialing by proxy, temporary privileges and emergency or disaster privileges run under separate procedures and are not described here.
Where our rules come from, and how to tell them apart
Larkhollow is a community hospital. It is not a federal facility. We adopted the verification standard work published by the Indian Health Service in its Medical Staff Credentialing and Privileging Standard Operating Procedure Manual, Version 8.0, September 2025, as our own written procedure, because it is a complete, current and publicly stated account of how the work is done.
Two kinds of sentence appear below, and each says which it is.
* Quoted from the manual, with the manual's own section number. We follow it.
* Larkhollow rule. Ours. Either the manual leaves the criterion open, or the manual's rule is tied to a federal facility and does not reach us. Where the manual says something different, or says nothing, the manual's own sentence is printed beside ours so that the difference is visible rather than buried.
Nothing below is a rule unless it is one of those two things. If you cannot find a rule here, ask the Medical Services Professional. Do not infer one from the manual, and do not invent one.
The office also runs identity verification, controlled-substance registrations, the National Practitioner Data Bank query, sanctions and exclusion lookups, life support certificates, continuing education, immunization records, liability coverage and malpractice history. Those are handled outside this procedure and are not part of the work described here.
1. Intake and completeness
We do not send the application before the offer is accepted. The manual, Section 5:
"Only after the applicant has accepted the tentative job offer can the full initial appointment application be sent to the applicant."
An application is taken up for processing only when it is complete. The manual, Section 5, opens its list with
"An application is complete and ready for import when:"
and names ten conditions, of which two govern almost everything else we do:
"a signed IHS Conditions of Application & Release is received (required to be able to conduct any verifications);"
"a request for specific privileges is received;"
Larkhollow rule. Our equivalent of that release is the Larkhollow Authorization and Release, printed inside the application. It is our own form; the manual's is a federal instrument and we do not use it. The rule it carries is the manual's and we keep it: until a signed release is on file we send no verification request of any kind. A file with no signed release cannot advance, no matter how much else is present.
Larkhollow rule — our completeness list. An application is complete when all nine hold:
1. the application is signed and dated by the applicant;
2. the Larkhollow Authorization and Release is signed and dated;
3. a request for specific privileges names at least one privilege group published in the current privilege criteria;
4. a current curriculum vitae is on file;
5. every professional practice question on the disclosure page is answered Yes or No, and every Yes carries the written explanation the form asks for;
6. the declared history runs continuously from the date the applicant finished professional school, with a written explanation for every period of 30 days or more that no entry covers;
7. at least two peer referees are named, with a working address for each;
8. every declared affiliation and employer carries a verification contact;
9. every licence and certification the applicant holds, active or inactive, is declared.
An item that is missing is requested from the applicant in writing, and the clock in the manual, Section 5, starts on the day we write:
"the LP has 30 calendar days to respond. After 30 calendar days, their application is considered incomplete and ineligible for processing."
Larkhollow rule. The 30 days run from the date on our written request, counted as calendar days, and the deadline day is included. A reply that arrives on day 30 is in time. A reply that adds or changes anything on the application arrives as a new revision of the application; we record it and keep the old one. A revision never overwrites what it replaces.
An unexplained gap does not go on a findings list. The manual, Section 6, Subsection 4, element 4:
"If the application is found to have any unexplained time period or gaps, the application will not be processed and will be returned to the applicant as incomplete."
2. Reconciliation
Before and during verification we read the curriculum vitae against the application, and then both against whatever the sources return. The manual, Section 6, Subsection 2:
"The MSP will compare the CV/resume with the application and completed verifications and correct or resolve any discrepancies."
"There must be a follow-up of any verification discrepancies found during the application and"
"The burden of proof is on the applicant to provide all necessary verifiable information to"
And Section 6, Subsection 4, element 3:
"If discrepancies exist, the applicant must provide a written explanation or be offered the opportunity to amend the submitted application."
Larkhollow rule — the office never picks a value. When the applicant says one thing and a source says another, we raise it and we record both. We do not decide which is right, we do not average them, and we do not quietly adopt the source's date because the source is the source. The applicant resolves it in writing or amends the application.
Larkhollow rule — a discrepancy holds its own entry and nothing else. A contested employment entry holds that entry. Every other entry on the file carries on being verified. But the file cannot be presented to the committee until the discrepancy is resolved, because presentation requires every element to be resolved (section 8 below).
Larkhollow rule — outstanding work does not stop the rest of the file. While one element of a file is outstanding, work on the other elements continues and their status is recorded; the office may hold the whole file instead only for a reason recorded in the file's action list; a file is never presented to the committee with an element outstanding.
Larkhollow rule — a revision is reconciled, not assumed. When a revision arrives, the reconciliation above runs again on what the revision says, against the curriculum vitae and against every verification already completed on the entries it touches. Dates are not the only thing a revision can move: the organization, the role, the supervisor and the verification contact all belong to the entry, and a change to any of them is a change to the entry. Section 11 says what re-opens when it does. The monitoring duty in section 11 runs alongside it and does not pause while a file waits.
3. The six checks
Six elements are verified in this procedure: licensure, experience, time gaps, professional education and post-graduate training, board certification, and professional peer references. The manual numbers seventeen essential credentialing elements in Section 6, Subsection 4. Of the other eleven, nine are handled by the office outside this procedure, as stated above; current competency is the clinical leadership's, not the office's; and the manual's conditions-and-release form is replaced by our own Authorization and Release, which is part of intake in this procedure.
What counts as a verification at all
The manual, Section 1, defines primary source verification as
"Verifying a credential from the original source"
and Section 6, Subsection 1 rules out two things we see constantly:
"Primary source verifications received directly from the applicant cannot be used."
"Copies of a diploma, license, registration, etc., in place of verifications are unacceptable."
A reply that reached us through the applicant is not a verification, however genuine the document looks, however clear the letterhead, however real the registrar's signature. It goes in the file as received and the request stays open.
A designated equivalent source is acceptable in place of the original. The manual leaves each of its lists open — Section 6, Subsection 4, element 2 ends
"etc., as long as the source is a designated equivalent source for education and training verifications"
and element 5 ends
"or other nationally recognized certifying body, as long as the source is a designated equivalent source for board certification verifications"
Larkhollow rule. An open list cannot be applied consistently, so ours is closed. The sources this office accepts for each element are named in attester-table.md. Anything not on that table is inadmissible and is raised to the Medical Services Professional. It is never quietly accepted as good enough, and it is never quietly downgraded to a secondary source.
There is one legitimate route to a weaker source, and it opens only on impossibility. The manual, Section 6, Subsection 1:
"If completing primary or DES verifications is impossible, such as when an educational institution or residency program has closed, secondary source verifications may be used."
"When a primary or designated equivalent source cannot be obtained, the applicant's recent affiliations should be contacted to discover how they obtained the verification."
Larkhollow rule. Impossibility is a closed school, a closed programme, a dissolved employer — a source that no longer exists to answer. A source that exists and does not answer is not impossible; it is non-responsive, and non-response is handled in section 4, not here. When the secondary path opens, the reason is written into the file.
How often we ask, and what silence means
The manual, Section 6, Subsection 2:
"Verifications are attempted at least three times."
"Each attempt, including whom it was attempted to verify with, the date of request, verification methods, and any additional comments, is documented in the Notes section of the entry."
"Note that non-responsive individuals or entities may be a red flag."
And Section 15, on affiliations:
"If the affiliation is unwilling to complete the verification or is non-responsive after 3 attempts, this should be noted as a red flag."
Larkhollow rule. The attempt log is permanent. A reply arriving on the fourth attempt does not erase the three that went unanswered — the record of how hard the file was to verify is part of the file. Silence is never a pass. An unanswered request is an outstanding item for as long as it stays unanswered.
Check 1 — Licensure
The manual, Section 6, Subsection 4, element 6:
"At the initial appointment, all active and inactive professional medical licenses will be verified."
"Licenses will be verified before expiration."
and, on what a licence has to be:
"Every licensed practitioner who provides patient care in federal facilities must possess a current, active, full, and unrestricted license or registration from a State, the District of Columbia, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or a territory of the United States."
Larkhollow rule — the practice state. The manual's sentence above is a federal facility's rule: it accepts a licence from any State, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico or a territory, and Section 15 says so again, answering the question "Where is it documented that a practitioner does not need to be licensed in the state where they provide services in a federal facility?" with
"Federal law at 25 U.S.C. § 1621t states that licensed health professionals employed by a tribal health program are exempt if licensed in any state, from the licensure requirements of the state where services under an ISDEAA agreement are performed."
We are not a federal facility and that exemption does not reach us. Larkhollow's bylaws require a practitioner to hold one current, active, full and unrestricted licence issued by the State of Washington, which is our practice state. Every other licence the applicant holds, active or inactive, in any state, is still verified under the manual's sentence above — we verify them all; only one of them satisfies the bylaw.
Larkhollow rule — full and unrestricted. A licence is not full and unrestricted when the board's record or the board's reply shows probation, supervision, a monitoring agreement, a practice limitation, a suspension, a stipulated condition or a surrender. A licence in any of those states is a finding and goes to the Clinical Director with its evidence. It is not the office's judgment whether the restriction matters.
The element's state is finding from the day the restriction is seen and stays finding on every later record of that revision, including after the Clinical Director's disposition ends the hold on the file. The disposition ends the wait; it does not turn a finding into a clean element. resolved is for an element with nothing to weigh.
Larkhollow rule — a National Provider Identifier is not a licence. It identifies a practitioner for billing. It says nothing about whether anybody is licensed. An applicant who declares an identifier in place of a licence has declared no licence.
Larkhollow rule — the cycle. An initial appointment at Larkhollow runs one year, matching the manual's Section 12:
"For IHS, initial appointments are one year long, and reappointments are two years long, regardless of accrediting body medical staff standards or medical staff bylaws."
The cycle starts on the date the appointment takes effect and ends one year later minus one day, so a cycle starting 2026-05-01 ends 2027-04-30. The Washington licence must be valid on the decision date. If it expires inside the cycle, that is not a denial and it is not a pass: it is recorded as a monitored condition with a re-verification due date set before the expiry date, and it does not block activation. If the re-verification fails, the file re-opens. The due date recorded on the condition is the licence's expiry date itself; "before" says when the re-verification must be complete, not what the recorded date is.
Check 2 — Experience and time gaps
The manual, Section 6, Subsection 4, element 3:
"At the initial appointment, relevant experience (affiliations, work history, and military) for at least the most recent five years for work history and the most recent five years for affiliation history"
"or as far back as necessary per any conflicting information or suspicious indicators—to assess current competency is verified."
Five years is a floor, not a ceiling. Conflicting information takes us further back.
Larkhollow rule — where the five years are measured from. The manual states the window and not its anchor. Ours is the date the application was first received: an entry is inside the window when any part of it falls in the five years counted back from the date the application was first received. A later revision does not move the anchor.
Element 4 defines a gap and says what is owed:
"A time gap is 30 or more days when the LP is not in school or training, in the military, teaching, working,"
"Verification of time gaps is not required, but an explanation is."
Larkhollow rule — how the gap list is computed. The clock starts on the day after the applicant finished professional school. Every declared entry of any type covers every day from its start date to its end date inclusive; an entry with no end date runs to the export date. An explanation names the period it covers, and it covers a gap only when that named period runs from at or before the gap's first day to at or after the gap's last day. A gap with a written explanation covering it is marked explained. A gap with no written explanation is unexplained, and the application is returned as incomplete under the manual's sentence quoted in section 1. "current competency is determined by clinical leadership, not the MSP."
Larkhollow rule — the long gap. Any gap of 180 days or more is routed to the Clinical Director for a recorded disposition, whether or not it carries an explanation. The Clinical Director decides; the office supplies the gap, the explanation and the verified dates.

"A qualifying degree is the degree required for the applicant's position and privileges."
"such as internship, residency, fellowship, or other organized professional training will be verified."
So: the qualifying degree, and every post-graduate training entry. The accepted sources are in attester-table.md. The admissibility rules are the ones in "What counts as a verification at all" above — the applicant may not carry the reply, and a source not on the table is raised.

Check 4 — Professional peer references
The manual, Section 6, Subsection 4, element 11:
"IHS policy requires the collection of at least two peer references at the initial appointment. The"
"All peer references are from a professional authority who has worked directly with the applicant within the past two years and can authoritatively speak to the applicant's character, clinical experience, and competency."
"the IHS definition of a peer includes a practitioner in the same clinical discipline."
"A peer must not be a relative, spouse, or partner."
Three disqualifiers, each independent: not worked together directly inside two years; not in the same clinical discipline; a relative, spouse or partner. A referee who fails any one of them does not count, and we find out only when the reply arrives and states the relationship.
Larkhollow rule — how each of the three is measured. The manual gives the conditions and not the arithmetic, so ours is:
* Worked together within two years is measured against the date the referee signs, because that is the day the referee attests to it. "Peer references are considered current if the reference's signature is within two years of the file presentation to the GB."
The signature date, not the date we received it. A reference can go stale while the file waits.

8. Packet readiness
The manual, Section 12:
"It is recommended that every file be audited before it goes through review."
and Section 8, on how long a verification stays good:
"Most of these verifications are required by accrediting organizations to be verified AT the time of appointment, the time between when the application is received and when it's reviewed."

Larkhollow rule — the usability window. A verification is usable when it was completed on or after the date this application was first received and before the decision date. There is no day count. Every one of the six elements resolved, no element outstanding, no discrepancy open, every verification inside the usability window, and the packet bound to one named application revision. Readiness is a fact about the revision's elements and nothing else. 2. Reconciliation
Before and during verification we read the curriculum vitae against the application, and then both against whatever the sources return. The manual, Section 6, Subsection 2:
"The MSP will compare the CV/resume with the application and completed verifications and correct or resolve any discrepancies."
"There must be a follow-up of any verification discrepancies found during the application and"
"The burden of proof is on the applicant to provide all necessary verifiable information to"
And Section 6, Subsection 4, element 3:
"If discrepancies exist, the applicant must provide a written explanation or be offered the opportunity to amend the submitted application."
Larkhollow rule — the office never picks a value. When the applicant says one thing and a source says another, we raise it and we record both. "Verifying a credential from the original source"

"Copies of a diploma, license, registration, etc., in place of verifications are unacceptable."
A reply that reached us through the applicant is not a verification, however genuine the document looks, however clear the letterhead, however real the registrar's signature. It goes in the file as received and the request stays open.

"etc., as long as the source is a designated equivalent source for education and training verifications"
and element 5 ends
"or other nationally recognized certifying body, as long as the source is a designated equivalent source for board certification verifications"

"When a primary or designated equivalent source cannot be obtained, the applicant's recent affiliations should be contacted to discover how they obtained the verification."
Larkhollow rule. Impossibility is a closed school, a closed programme, a dissolved employer — a source that no longer exists to answer. 8. Packet readiness
The manual, Section 12:
"It is recommended that every file be audited before it goes through review."
and Section 8, on how long a verification stays good:
"Most of these verifications are required by accrediting organizations to be verified AT the time of appointment, the time between when the application is received and when it's reviewed."
The manual gave a fixed number once and removed it: its own change log for Version 5.0 records "Section 8: Removed 120-day expiration of primary source verifications."
Larkhollow rule — the usability window. A verification is usable when it was completed on or after the date this application was first received and before the decision date. There is no day count. The anchor is the date revision 1 arrived, not the date of the current revision, so a later revision does not by itself void every verification already completed — what a revision invalidates is decided entry by entry, by reading what the revision actually changed. Peer references carry the additional two-year signature rule in check 4, which is stricter and wins where the two disagree.
Larkhollow rule — the board lookup and the window. A board lookup is the office's own check of the state board's public record on a day of the office's choosing, not a reply from a source, so the usability window is not applied to it: a lookup run on the decision day is usable for that decision. The date a packet became presentable is the date the last verification reply it needed was received; the lookup does not set it.
Larkhollow rule — what makes a packet presentable. Every one of the six elements resolved, no element outstanding, no discrepancy open, every verification inside the usability window, and the packet bound to one named application revision. Readiness is computed from the element statuses, not from anybody's recollection that the file looked finished.
For readiness, resolved means the element has nothing left to verify. An element carrying a finding is resolved in that sense once its evidence is with the Clinical Director — a licensure finding once the Clinical Director's disposition is on file, a certification finding on part of the request at once — and the packet is presented with the finding on it. An eligibility question, a gap awaiting the Clinical Director's disposition, an open discrepancy, an item returned to the applicant and a high-risk finding without its disposition are not resolved: while any of them stands, the packet is not presentable.
A packet is a statement about one revision at one moment. If any element re-opens, readiness for that revision is gone, and the earlier readiness record stays in the file as history.
Readiness is a fact about the revision's elements and nothing else. A refused decision record does not undo it, and a withdrawn or discontinued file keeps the readiness its revision had: the office records what was ready, whatever the file did next. Only an element re-opening or a new revision changes it.
9. The committee protocol
The medical staff recommends; the Governing Body approves. The manual, Section 1:
"The Governing Body has the authority to grant, modify, or deny medical staff membership and clinical privileges to LPs"
and the Executive Committee of the Medical Staff
"proposes a recommendation through the clinical director (CD) and the chief executive officer (CEO) or their designee to the Governing Body"
Section 7:
"The GB or a delegated GB committee retains the final authority to grant, renew, or deny privileges after considering the recommendations of the medical staff"
Section 12, on who may record what:
"All signatories should utilize a "recommend" selection, with only the Chair of the GB or their designee using the "approval" selection."
A recommendation is not an approval. A record from the Credentials Committee or the Executive Committee of the Medical Staff that carries the word "approved" is still a recommendation, because those bodies cannot approve. Only the Governing Body chair, or the designee named in authority-roster.md, records an approval.
Larkhollow rule — what makes a decision admissible. All five, checked against the roster and the packet and never against the record's own claim:
1. the body is one that may record that outcome;
2. the signatory held the named role on the decision date, per authority-roster.md;
3. the decision names the same applicant and the same application revision as the presentable packet;
4. a presentable packet existed for that revision before the decision date;
5. the outcome is one of approved, approved-with-conditions, deferred-pending-information, denied, recommended, not recommended, and every outcome other than a plain approval carries a reason.
A decision that fails any of these is not a decision. It is recorded as received, raised to the Medical Services Professional, and nothing activates on it.
Larkhollow rule — a decision against a superseded revision. It does not authorize the current revision. It stays in the file as history against the revision it named, and it is never deleted.
Larkhollow rule — two decisions for one revision. A second decision for the same application revision is admissible only when it names the earlier decision it supersedes. Without that reference it is a duplicate, it is inadmissible, and it is raised to the Medical Services Professional. The first decision continues to stand.
Larkhollow rule — which outcomes carry a reason, and what counts as a second decision. recommended is the positive outcome of a body that cannot approve (the Credentials Committee or the Executive Committee of the Medical Staff); like a plain approval it carries no reason, while not recommended carries one, as do approval-with-conditions, deferral and denial. The two-decisions rule above applies to a second decision of the same body for the same revision: a recommendation followed by the Governing Body's decision on the same revision is the normal sequence, not a duplicate, and a second recommendation is never a duplicate — so in practice it is a second Governing Body decision for the same revision that must name the earlier one it supersedes.
Larkhollow rule — deferral. A deferral names the information it waits for. The office chases exactly that, and the file does not advance while it waits.
10. Activation and the appointment cycle
The manual, Section 5:
"The provider cannot provide patient care services until the practitioner has been approved for their next appointment and privilege cycle."
and Section 15:
"The GB needs to approve a provider's privileges and/or appointment on or before the"
expiry date, to prevent a lapse; and a later start date is permitted when the body records it:
"Yes, if the GB makes the notation in their final notes when they sign off on the signature pages in Virtual Committee."
Larkhollow rule — activation. On an admitted Governing Body approval, the office records the appointment and activates exactly the privilege groups named in the decision — never more, and never a group that was requested but not granted. Privileges become active on the effective date the decision records, or on the decision date when the decision records no separate effective date. Nothing is active before that day. The cycle end is computed as in check 1.
Larkhollow rule — approve with conditions. An approval with conditions activates the approved privilege groups on the normal rule above, and records each condition as a monitored condition with its own due date. 11. Re-entry: when something lands on work already done
The manual, Section 15:
"The MSP must verify all expirables upon expiration and place the documentation in the file."
"must continue monitoring expirables even during the review process and always provide the most current information"

Larkhollow rule — the five re-entry triggers, and what each affects:
What arrives
	What it affects
	A new application revision
	intake and completeness run again on the new revision; the prior revision stays in the file; any packet readiness bound to the prior revision is gone
	New evidence on an element — a reply, a reclassification, a corrected date
	that element re-opens; packet readiness is gone; other elements are untouched
	A credential expires or is renewed
	the licensure check re-runs on the new dates; a re-verification is placed in the file
	A decision that is not admissible, or that names a superseded revision
	nothing activates; the record is raised, kept, and never deleted
	A withdrawal by the applicant, or a discontinuation by the Clinical Director
	the file ends with the terminal reason recorded. It is never labelled appointed
	A re-entry adds an occurrence to the file. It does not overwrite the occurrence before it.","id":"REDACTED","parent_ids":null,"drive_id":null,"created_time":"2026-09-24T07:01:51.663Z","modified_time":"2026-09-24T07:01:52.694Z","is_empty":false,"mime_type":"text/plain","file_name":null,"file_size_bytes":null,"url":"https://drive.google.com/file/d/REDACTED"}},"isError":false}

﻿How this office exports its credentialing records
Larkhollow Community Hospital · Medical Staff Office A note from the Medical Services Professional to whoever automates the initial-appointment file. Written 2026-03-16, alongside the first export.
I run the export from the credentialing database every few weeks and drop it in the shared folder, one sub-folder per export. Here is what you get, what the columns mean, and the three or four things that catch people out.
The export date is the clock
Every batch folder has a README.md that says the export date and the window it covers. That date is the clock for everything in the folder: nothing in a batch happened after its export date. Work the batch as if today were the export date. Do not use the real date you run your tool, and do not carry today's date into an arithmetic that a batch is supposed to settle.
The three exports are 2026-03-16, 2026-04-20 and 2026-05-18. The first one covers everything on file up to and including 2026-03-15, however far back it goes — one application here was first received in 2024. The second and third cover only what changed since the previous one.
The caseload at an export date is every application file the office has received up to that date, however that file ended. A withdrawn or discontinued file stays in the caseload with its final status; a later batch never removes a file, it only adds to what is known about it.
A batch is closed. It never changes.
I never go back and edit an export. If an applicant corrects something, a new revision of the application appears in a later batch and the old one stays exactly where it was. If a board sends a corrected reply, the corrected reply is a new row and the old row stays. If a committee decides something twice, there are two decision records.
So: do not diff a later batch against an earlier one looking for edits. There are none. What a later batch contains is new rows, new documents and new observations.
The files
Thirteen comma-separated exports, and three folders of documents.
File
	One row is
	applications.csv
	an application revision I received in the window
	application-disclosures.csv
	one professional practice question and the applicant's answer
	declared-history.csv
	one history entry the applicant declared
	declared-credentials.csv
	one licence or certification as the applicant described it
	privilege-requests.csv
	one privilege group requested
	licence-lookup-wa.csv
	one Washington credential record from the state board's lookup
	licence-lookup-other-states.csv
	one out-of-state credential record
	certification-replies.csv
	one certifying board's reply
	verification-replies.csv
	one reply about education and training, or about an affiliation or employer
	verification-attempts.csv
	one request I sent
	peer-referees.csv
	one referee named on an application, or supplied later
	peer-reference-replies.csv
	one completed reference form that came back
	correspondence.csv
	one letter, memo or decision record, with the path to the document
	

Folder
	What is in it
	letters/
	applicants' explanation letters, withdrawals, referee substitutions, and my own written requests for missing items
	dispositions/
	the Clinical Director's recorded dispositions
	decisions/
	Credentials Committee and Executive Committee minutes extracts, and Governing Body approval records
	correspondence.csv is an index. It tells you the documents exist and where they are. It does not tell you what they say — you have to open them.
A file with only a header row means the export ran and there was nothing in that window. That is not the same as a missing file, and it is not an error.
Dates, blanks and columns
* Dates are YYYY-MM-DD. Always. A date range is inclusive at both ends: an entry from_date 2022-01-01, to_date 2022-12-31 covers the 1st of January and the 31st of December. An expiry date is the last day the credential is valid.
* An empty cell means I hold no value for that field. It does not mean zero, it does not mean "no", and it does not mean the answer is unknown-but-probably-fine. Two blanks carry a specific meaning and you should learn them:
   * a blank to_date in declared-history.csv means the entry is current, running to the export date — not that the end date is missing;
   * a blank expiry_date in certification-replies.csv means the certificate does not expire — some older certificates are time-unlimited.
* No money appears anywhere. We do not record fees, salaries or contract values in the credentialing file.
* Files are UTF-8 with Unix line endings. Values are quoted only when they contain a comma.
The three joins that matter
1. Everything on the applicant side joins on application_id, and on revision where the fact belongs to a revision. Entries, credentials, privilege requests and disclosures all restate on each revision, so always filter to the revision you are working.
2. The Washington board export carries no practitioner identifier. It never has. I join it to an application on lastname, firstname, middlename and birthyear. I have checked that no two rows in any one export share those four values, so the join gives you at most one row. An applicant with no row in that file holds no Washington credential. The absence is the answer, not a data problem.
3. A referee with no row in peer-reference-replies.csv has not replied. Silence produces no record. You can see it only by looking at the requests in verification-attempts.csv and finding no reply against them.
The Washington export's own columns
I pass that file through as the board publishes it and add one column. The board's twelve are credentialnumber, credentialtype, status, firstissuedate, lastissuedate, expirationdate, ceduedate, actiontaken, birthyear, firstname, middlename, lastname. Mine is lookup_date — the day I ran the lookup. It is my own act, not a source's reply, so the usability window is not applied to it.
Two of the board's columns are easy to misread:
* ceduedate is a continuing-education due date. We do not use it. Continuing education is handled outside this procedure and it has nothing to do with whether a licence is valid.
* actiontaken says the board has acted. It does not say what the action was. For that you need the board's written reply, which arrives as a document, not in this file. A Yes here is a reason to go and read; it is not a conclusion.
The first export carries the board's whole file for our county — 435 rows — so you can see what an ordinary population looks like. The second and third carry only a re-lookup of the practitioners whose files are open, because that is all I re-run.
How often anything is actually wrong
I want to say this plainly, because a small sample of credentialing files can leave the wrong impression.
In the board's population, action against a credential is rare. In the 435-row export you have: 431 rows say No, 3 say Yes, and 1 says Pending. That is 0.69% Yes and 0.23% Pending, and it is the shape of the real thing — the overwhelming majority of licensed practitioners have a clean board record, and any tool that expects otherwise will be wrong almost every time it fires.
The applicants in these batches are a different matter, and deliberately so. This is a teaching set. I have put every situation the procedure has a rule for into these three exports on purpose, so the run has something to exercise: a restricted licence, an unexplained gap, a school that closed, a referee who never answers, a certificate that lapsed, a decision against the wrong revision. A real nine weeks of intake would be far quieter than this. Do not read the applicant set as a base rate. Read it as a checklist that happens to be shaped like a caseload.
The clean files are genuinely clean. If your tool raises something on one of them, it is your tool.
What I do not export
My own queue, my own statuses and my own conclusions. This export is the evidence, not my reading of it. What is complete, what is outstanding, what is presentable and what is owed to whom is the work — it is not in the folder, and it should not be.
Referee addresses. The export carries no address column for peer referees. The working-address half of completeness condition 7 is checked by my office outside the export, so a run assesses condition 7 on the named referees alone and records the address check as not assessable from the export — neither met nor failed.
